about: The citizens of the city of Rome (places_rome.gd, citizen.gd): names, the jobs they walk the city at (docs/rome-jobs.md has the full list), and what they say. {name} is their name, {home} the part of the city they live in, {partner} and {kids} their family, {patron} the great house they belong to.

jobs.title: baker
jobs.intro: {name}. I've got the bakery with the donkey mill, round the corner. You'll have smelled it.
work: Up in the dark, every day. The donkeys turn the millstones, I knead, the boy stokes the oven.
Good bread wants a hot oven and a cold baker. I have the one, never the other.
Every loaf gets my stamp before it goes in. That way nobody can say a bad one was mine.
worry: If the grain ships are late from Egypt, flour doubles overnight and they shout at me, not at the grain men.

jobs.title: miller
jobs.intro: {name}. I work the mill boats down on the river.
work: The Goths cut the aqueducts, so the old mills stopped. Belisarius had mills put on boats in the Tiber. The current turns them now.
When the river's high we grind all night. When it's low, we wait and pray.
worry: If they cut the river too, we're done for.

jobs.title: butcher
jobs.intro: {name}, butcher. Pork's my trade, and beef when the cattle market has any worth having.
work: Sausages, trotters, a nice bit of belly. The rich want the udders of a sow. I don't ask.
The knife's the easy part. It's keeping the flies off in summer that makes you old.
The meat left over from the sacrifices comes to us to sell. The gods take the smoke, we take the rest.
worry: My landlord wants the rent on the Kalends, whether the pigs came in or not.

jobs.title: fishmonger
jobs.intro: {name}. Fish. You can tell from the smell, can't you?
work: Mullet in the morning, eels in the evening. If it came up the Tiber after dark, I'd rather not sell it.
The rich pay a fortune for a big mullet. They fight over it at the auctions like it's a racehorse.
Salt fish from Spain keeps. Fresh fish is gone by noon or it's gone off.
worry: The fish between the bridges comes out of the drain of the city. The good stuff comes up from Ostia.

jobs.title: greengrocer
jobs.intro: {name}. I grow them myself, out past the gate, and bring them in on the donkey.
work: Cabbage is the best thing in the world. Cato said so, and he was never wrong about a vegetable.
Leeks, lettuces, beans, turnips. Whatever the season gives, that's what you eat.
I'm in at dawn, sold out by noon, home by dark. It's a good life if it doesn't rain.
worry: The carts on the road at night, the noise, the thieves. My knees are going too.

jobs.title: fruit seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Figs, apples, pears, whatever's ripe.
work: Figs from Tusculum, the best. Taste one. Go on.
Apples keep through the winter if you store them right. I know the right way and I'm not telling.
worry: The wasps in autumn. They get the figs before the customers do.

jobs.title: oil seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Oil. For lamps, for cooking, for the baths. You need oil for everything.
work: The best comes from Venafrum, the cheap stuff from Spain. I sell both and I tell you which is which. Mostly.
Every jar that comes up the river ends up on the big pile of broken ones by the port. A hill of pots, going up every year.
worry: A cracked jar in the storeroom and a month's profit runs into the drain.

jobs.title: wine seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Wine. Falernian if you've money, the house red if you haven't.
work: Always mix it with water. Only barbarians drink it neat.
The Greeks put resin in theirs. The Gauls drink beer. Pity them.
A merchant from Campania comes up every month. His jars are sealed with pitch, so you can trust them, almost.
worry: The aediles came round checking my measures again. As if I'd cheat. Much.

jobs.title: innkeeper
jobs.intro: {name}, and this is my inn. Beds upstairs, a jug and a stew down here.
work: The carters come in at night and the drovers at dawn. I sleep in between, when I sleep.
Travellers write on my walls. Some of it's even polite.
Dice in the back room? I don't know what you're talking about. The aediles don't either.
worry: People say innkeepers water the wine. People say a lot of things.

jobs.title: cook-shop keeper
jobs.intro: {name}. Hot food at my counter, all day. Chickpeas, lentils, a bit of sausage.
work: Most people up in the flats can't cook: no kitchen, and the landlord won't have a fire. So they eat at mine.
The pots sit in the counter, over the coals. Point at what you want, pay, eat. Simple.
worry: The rich say places like mine are where the idle and the wicked go. They've never been hungry at noon.

jobs.title: sausage seller
jobs.intro: {name}. Sausages. I sell them hot from the tray, all over.
work: You shout, you walk, you shout. The baths are the best: everyone comes out hungry.
worry: My voice is going. Too much shouting, not enough wine.

jobs.title: pastry cook
jobs.intro: {name}. Cakes with honey, cakes with cheese, little cakes for the gods.
work: Honey cakes for the children, cheese cakes for the priests, the best ones for the rich man's dinner.
Libum, now: cheese, flour, an egg, bay leaves under it. You bake it for someone's birthday, for his genius.
worry: Honey's so dear this year. The bees don't care what I charge.

jobs.title: water carrier
jobs.intro: {name}. I carry water up to the top floors for the ones who pay.
work: The fountain's down here, the family's up on the fifth floor. Up and down, all day. My legs are like a mule's.
Rich houses have a pipe from the aqueduct right into the house. The rest of us have me.
worry: If the fountain runs dry, they blame me, as if I drank it all.

jobs.title: fuller
jobs.intro: {name}, fuller. I clean togas. You'd be amazed what gets on a toga.
work: We tread the cloth in the vats with fuller's earth and urine. Yes, urine. There's a pot for it on every corner, and I pay for it.
Our guild has its own feast day, the Quinquatrus, for Minerva. We drink to her and to the vats.
Then we card it, bleach it over sulphur, and press it. White as snow when it goes back.
worry: The smell? You stop noticing after twenty years. Your wife never does.

jobs.title: cobbler
jobs.intro: {name}, cobbler. Sit down, show me your feet. Hm. Those won't last the month.
work: Soldiers' boots, ladies' slippers, senators' red shoes with the little moon on them. I make the lot.
Hobnails in the sole. Wears them longer and it makes a racket on the paving. The soldiers love it.
worry: Leather's gone up again. The tanners across the river do what they like.

jobs.title: clothes dealer
jobs.intro: {name}. Tunics, cloaks, the odd toga for a funeral. New and second-hand.
work: The Vicus Tuscus is where you buy clothes. Everyone knows. The best stock is mine.
Wool from Tarentum is the softest. The cheap rough stuff is for slaves and it itches.
worry: Thieves at the baths steal clothes off the benches. Then they come and try to sell them to me.

jobs.title: weaver
jobs.intro: {name}. I weave. My mother did, and hers.
work: The loom stands upright, the weights pull the threads straight. Clack, clack, all day.
A good woman works wool, the old tombstones say. Mine will say I worked it better than anyone on this street.
worry: My eyes. You squint at threads for thirty years, then you can't see the street.

jobs.title: purple dealer
jobs.intro: {name}, from Tyre. Purple, the real thing, from the shellfish.
work: Ten thousand shells for a little dye. That's why a senator's stripe costs what it costs.
There's cheap purple from plants. You can tell the moment the sun hits it.
worry: The laws against luxury come and go. When they come, nobody buys.

jobs.title: blacksmith
jobs.intro: {name}. Smith. Knives, hinges, nails, cramps for the builders.
work: Iron from Noricum is the best. I don't often get it.
Vulcan's my god. You don't want to be on the wrong side of the god of your own fire.
worry: The neighbours complain about the hammering. The neighbours can live in the country.

jobs.title: goldsmith
jobs.intro: {name}. Goldsmith, on the Sacred Way, like all the good ones.
work: Rings, brooches, a little gold leaf for the gods' statues. The work's small, the price isn't.
My master taught me when I was a slave. When he freed me, I took his name and his customers.
worry: You can't turn your back for a moment. Gold walks.

jobs.title: potter
jobs.intro: {name}. Pots. Cooking pots, jugs, lamps if you want.
work: The clay's from the river valley. The kiln's outside the wall, because of the fires.
The fancy red ware comes from Arretium, stamped with the maker's name. Mine's for using, not for showing off.
worry: Every pot that cracks in the kiln is a meal I don't eat.

jobs.title: lamp maker
jobs.intro: {name}. Oil lamps. Two moulds, clay in the middle, bake them. Simple.
work: Gladiators on the top, the gods, a pair of lovers. People like a picture on their lamp.
One nozzle for the poor, three for the rich. Same oil, more smoke.
worry: Everyone's got a lamp already. Luckily they keep breaking them.

jobs.title: perfumer
jobs.intro: {name}. Perfumes, oils, ointments. The best noses in Rome come to me.
work: Rose from Campania, nard from India, saffron. It costs more than silver, weight for weight.
The rich men wear more of it than the women now. Don't say I said so.
worry: The old men in the Senate want to ban it. They smell like goats and think it's virtue.

jobs.title: bookseller
jobs.intro: {name}. Books. New ones are posted on the pillars outside. Come in, have a look.
work: I've got slaves copying all day. Twenty copies of a new poem by the Nones.
Poets hate me. They say I get rich and they get fame. They're right.
worry: Mice. They eat the glue. The glue! Then the whole book falls apart.

jobs.title: money changer
jobs.intro: {name}. I change money and I test coin. Show me that, let me ring it on the table.
work: A bad coin rings flat. Silver-plated copper. There's more of it about than you'd think.
Greek drachmas, Egyptian ones, the new coin from the mint. I know them all by the ring.
worry: When the mint cheapens the silver, everyone blames the man at the table. Me.

jobs.title: barber
jobs.intro: {name}, barber. Sit, sit. A shave, a trim? You look like a philosopher, no offence.
work: A barber hears everything. Who's in debt, who's in love, who's in trouble with the praetor.
Razor, water, no soap. If I cut you, a cobweb soaked in vinegar stops it. Don't worry.
worry: The young ones all want beards now, like the Greeks. Terrible for business.

jobs.title: doctor
jobs.intro: {name}, a doctor, from Pergamon, trained in the Greek way.
work: Most of what I do is tell people to eat less, walk more and stay out of the Tiber.
Romans didn't used to have doctors. They had cabbage and their grandfathers' remedies. Some still do.
worry: If a patient dies, it's my fault. If he lives, it was the gods.

jobs.title: midwife
jobs.intro: {name}. I'm a midwife. Half this street came into the world through my hands.
work: The birthing stool, warm oil, clean cloth, a steady voice. The rest is the gods and the mother.
They call me at any hour. Babies don't come by the water clock.
worry: Not every one lives. You remember those ones more.

jobs.title: schoolmaster
jobs.intro: {name}. I teach letters and sums, there, under the awning, from dawn till noon.
work: The boys chant their letters, the neighbours shout at us to shut up, we chant louder.
A cane helps. I don't like it. Their fathers do.
worry: Half of them don't pay on time, and I can't keep the boy back for his father's debts.

jobs.title: boy's tutor
jobs.intro: {name}. I'm the young master's paedagogus. I take him to school and I make sure he gets there.
work: Greek in the morning, manners all day. I'm a Greek myself, so I'm cheap to keep and good for his accent.
When he's grown he'll forget me. They always do. Some free you. That's the hope.
worry: If he falls in the street, it's my back that gets the beating.

jobs.title: crier
jobs.intro: {name}! Crier and auctioneer! You need something shouted? I'm your man.
work: Auctions, lost slaves, games announced, laws posted: I shout it all in the Forum.
It's a trade despised by the fine folk and it's made more men rich than their estates have.
worry: You lose your voice, you lose your living.
call: Hear ye! Auction at noon by the Temple of Castor!
Games next month! The aediles give games!

jobs.title: carpenter
jobs.intro: {name}. Carpenter. I build floors and roofs, and the frames for the concrete.
work: They build them six storeys high and want them cheap. I build what I'm paid for.
Our guild's the biggest in Rome. We've got a meeting house, a feast on our holiday, and a burial fund.
worry: When a block comes down, they always blame the carpenter first and the owner never.

jobs.title: marble mason
jobs.intro: {name}. Marble. I cut it, I polish it, I set it.
work: It comes in blocks up the river: white from Luna, yellow from Numidia, purple from Egypt.
In the Republic they built in tufa and plaster. Now they want marble on everything.
worry: The dust gets in your chest. Old masons all cough.

jobs.title: wall painter
jobs.intro: {name}. I paint walls. Red panels, black, a garden with birds if you pay for it.
work: You paint while the plaster's wet, so it lasts. Once it dries, the colour's in the wall for good.
Cinnabar red costs a fortune. The owner supplies it himself so we can't steal any.
worry: Some owners want a whole seaside villa painted on a wall the size of a door.

jobs.title: plasterer
jobs.intro: {name}. Plasterer. Three coats of lime and sand, then three of marble dust. That's how you do it properly.
work: It's cheap work if it's done badly and good work if it's done slowly. Nobody wants slow.
worry: The lime eats your hands.

jobs.title: porter
jobs.intro: {name}. I carry things. That's it. Where to?
work: A sack of flour, a jar of oil, a bed up four flights. It's all the same to my back.
No carts in the city by day, so everything goes on somebody's shoulders. Mine, mostly.
worry: The steps up to the Capitol. They'll be the death of me.

jobs.title: sack carrier
jobs.intro: {name}. I unload the grain barges down at the port.
work: Sixty pounds a sack, off the barge, into the warehouse, and the clerk marks a tally for each.
It all comes up from Ostia, from the big ships from Egypt and Africa. Rome eats that much.
worry: The clerk miscounts. Always against us, funnily enough.

jobs.title: muleteer
jobs.intro: {name}. Muleteer. I bring the carts in at night. Wheels on the stones, all night long.
work: Carts aren't allowed in by day. So Rome sleeps badly and eats well.
worry: My mule's cleverer than I am and more stubborn than my wife.

jobs.title: litter bearer
jobs.intro: {name}. I carry my master's litter. Eight of us. Big Syrians, if he can afford them.
work: He reads and sleeps inside. We sweat outside. Such is life.
worry: The Clivus Capitolinus with the master inside. Uphill both ways, somehow.

jobs.title: boatman
jobs.intro: {name}. I run a boat on the Tiber. Ferry, barge, whatever pays.
work: Against the current it's the oxen on the towpath that do the work. Downstream it's the river.
Ostia and back, two days, if the river's kind.
worry: Floods in spring. The river comes up into the Forum some years.

jobs.title: bath keeper
jobs.intro: {name}. I run the baths, the little ones down the street. A quarter of an as.
work: Cold room, warm room, hot room. The slaves keep the furnace going under the floor all day.
Women in the morning, men in the afternoon, at mine. At the big ones they have their own rooms.
worry: People steal clothes. People pee in the pool. People are people.

jobs.title: diviner
jobs.intro: {name}, haruspex, from Etruria. I read the liver of the victim.
work: Each part of the liver belongs to a god. If it's swollen here, bad news. If it's clean, good.
Senators hire me. Generals hire me. Then they do what they wanted anyway.
worry: Some young men laugh at the old arts. They stop laughing when the lightning strikes.

jobs.title: temple keeper
jobs.intro: {name}. I keep this temple. I open it, sweep it, and keep an eye on the offerings.
work: People leave all sorts: little clay feet when a foot's healed, cakes, coins, wishes on lead.
At festivals it's full. On ordinary days it's me and the pigeons and the god.
worry: The pigeons are no respecters of gods.

jobs.title: sacrificial attendant
jobs.intro: {name}. I lead the beasts to the altar and see they go quietly.
work: A beast that goes willing is a good sign. So you don't pull. You coax.
The gods get the smoke and the insides, and the people get a feast out of the rest.
worry: If the ox bolts at the altar, it's a bad omen and they start the whole thing over.

jobs.title: undertaker
jobs.intro: {name}. Undertaker. We don't take it personally when people avoid us.
work: Mourners, pipers, torch bearers, the pyre outside the walls. I arrange the whole thing.
Poor folk pay into a burial club, a few coins a month, so they get a proper send-off.
worry: Nobody wants to talk to the undertaker. Until they need one.

jobs.title: piper
jobs.intro: {name}. Piper. Weddings, funerals, sacrifices. Rome can't do anything without a pipe.
work: At a sacrifice, the pipe drowns out any bad word said by mistake. That's what I'm for.
Once the pipers went on strike and walked out to Tibur. The Senate got them back drunk in carts.
worry: Funerals are steady work. I'd rather do weddings.

jobs.title: street performer
jobs.intro: {name}! Actor, singer, juggler, whatever you'll pay to see.
work: The real theatre's for the proper actors. The street's for me. The street pays better.
I do the jealous husband, the stupid slave and the greedy old man. Everyone's seen them, everyone laughs.
worry: The aediles move us on if we're too rude. Rude is what they laugh at hardest.

jobs.title: charioteer
jobs.intro: {name}. I drive for the Greens. You've heard of me. No? You will.
work: Four horses, seven laps, the turning posts close enough to touch. That's where men die.
Win enough and they free you, and the crowd knows your name, and the rich invite you to dinner.
worry: The Blues put a curse tablet on my horses. Buried it right under the starting gate. I know it.

jobs.title: gladiator
jobs.intro: {name}. Thracian style. Small shield, curved sword. I've fought eleven times.
work: Most fights, the loser lives if he fought well. The crowd decides, and the man giving the games.
We eat barley and beans at the school, to put a layer of fat on. They call us barley men.
worry: If I make it to the wooden sword, I'm free. Three more fights. Maybe four.

jobs.title: gladiator trainer
jobs.intro: {name}. I own a troupe of gladiators. The best in the city, so I tell the magistrates.
work: I hire them out to men giving games. Every one who dies, I get paid for. Handsomely.
People look down on my trade. Then they buy tickets.
worry: Feeding them costs a fortune. Barley men, they eat like horses.

jobs.title: clerk
jobs.intro: {name}. Clerk of the treasury, under the Temple of Saturn. The state's accounts go through my hands.
work: Magistrates come and go every year. We stay. We know where everything is.
Wax tablets for the drafts, papyrus for the records, bronze for the laws.
worry: A new quaestor every year who thinks he knows better. Every single year.

jobs.title: lictor
jobs.intro: {name}. Lictor. I carry the rods before the magistrate. Make way.
work: Inside the city the axe stays out of the rods, because a citizen can appeal to the people.
Twelve before a consul, six before a praetor. We go in single file and people step aside.
worry: Standing about in the heat while the magistrate talks. That's most of it.

jobs.title: watchman
jobs.intro: {name}. Of the watch, the vigiles. Fire's our business, and thieves at night.
work: Buckets, axes, hooks for pulling down a burning wall, blankets soaked in vinegar.
Seven cohorts, a station for every two regions. Most of us are freedmen. Six years' service and you're a citizen.
worry: The top floors of those insulae. A lamp tips over and forty families are on the street.

jobs.title: soldier
jobs.intro: {name}. Soldier. I keep order, as ordered.
work: We walk the streets, we stand at the games, we break up fights. Boring, mostly. Better than the frontier.
Pay's on time here in the city. That's why every man in the army wants a posting to Rome.
worry: Some nights it's all brawls and burning. Some nights it's nothing, and those are worse, waiting.

jobs.title: senator
jobs.intro: I am {name}. My family has sat in the Senate for generations.
work: The morning is for my clients, the afternoon for the Senate or the courts, the evening for dinner. There's no rest in being important.
You don't trade, as a senator. It's beneath us. We own land. And sometimes the men who trade.
worry: Elections cost more every year. My father bought votes cheaper.

jobs.title: client
jobs.intro: {name}. I'm a client of the house of {patron}. You'll have heard of them.
work: At dawn I put on my toga and go and greet my patron. He gives me a little basket of food, or some coins.
I walk behind him to the Forum. The more of us, the greater he looks. That's my job, if you like.
worry: The toga's hot, the patron's late, and the basket's smaller than last year.

jobs.title: householder
jobs.intro: I'm {name}. I run my husband's household, and I run it well.
work: The slaves, the stores, the children, the accounts. Men think a house runs itself.
I go to the temple of Bona Dea, the Good Goddess. Men aren't allowed. That suits us fine.
worry: My son wants to go into politics. It costs everything we have.

jobs.title: maid
jobs.intro: {name}. I'm a maid in the house of {patron}. I'm out for the shopping.
work: Fish, bread, oil, and the mistress's thread from the Vicus Tuscus. And I'm back before she notices I stopped to talk.
Some houses are kind. Mine is kind enough.
worry: I'm saving my allowance. Twelve years, maybe, and I can buy myself free.

jobs.title: slave
jobs.intro: {name}. I belong to the house of {patron}. I run errands for the steward.
work: Letters to deliver, a message to a friend, the bread. I know every shortcut in Rome.
My master's not bad. The steward is the one you watch out for.
worry: They say if I work hard I'll be freed before I'm thirty. They say a lot of things.

jobs.title: merchant
jobs.intro: {name}. A merchant. Glass and cloth from Syria, and I buy wine to take back.
work: Rome has everything, because everything comes here. And it all has to be paid for.
Sea from Antioch to Puteoli, road to Rome. Six weeks if the gods are kind.
worry: Pirates, storms, customs men. Customs men are the worst.

jobs.title: priest
jobs.intro: {name}, a priest of the church of this quarter.
work: On the Lord's day we meet at dawn. On the other days, the sick, the widows, the ones in debt.
The bishop sends bread to the poor through us. There's always less bread than poor.
worry: The old families still sacrifice to their old gods behind closed doors. We pray for them.

jobs.title: deacon
jobs.intro: {name}, deacon. I see to the food for the poor.
work: The church's farms send grain and wine. We give it out here on the steps.
Seven regions of the city, seven deacons. We keep lists, name by name.
worry: When the grain doesn't come, the lists are all we have to give out.

jobs.title: monk
jobs.intro: {name}. A monk. We keep the psalms, day and night.
work: We pray at the hours, work with our hands, eat once a day.
People bring us their sick. We nurse them. Sometimes they live.
worry: The world is ending, some of the brothers say. Look around. They may be right.

jobs.title: catacomb digger
jobs.intro: {name}. I dig the galleries outside the walls where the Christians are buried.
work: Down in the tufa with a lamp and a pick. Shelf after shelf, gallery below gallery.
The martyrs are buried down there. Pilgrims come to pray at their tombs.
worry: The Goths went through the cemeteries looking for gold. There's no gold. Only bones and prayers.

jobs.title: beggar
jobs.intro: {name}. Nobody. A beggar. Spare something?
work: I was a baker once, when there were people to buy bread.
The church steps are best. The Christians have to give, it's in their book.
worry: Winter. Winter's what I worry about.

jobs.title: pilgrim
jobs.intro: {name}. A pilgrim, come to pray at the tomb of Peter.
work: I walked from Gaul. Four months. My feet are all blisters and my heart is full.
Peter across the river, Paul out on the Ostian Way, and all the martyrs in the catacombs.
worry: The roads aren't safe. Goths, bandits, hunger. We came anyway.

jobs.title: foreigner
jobs.intro: {name}. Not from here, as you can tell by my accent.
work: I came for work and stayed. Half the city came from somewhere else.
In my country the food is better and the rents are lower. But this is Rome.
worry: Some Romans think anyone who isn't Roman is a fool. Some Romans are fools.

jobs.title: citizen of the plebs
jobs.intro: {name}. Citizen. No land, no money, but a citizen.
work: I take the grain dole each month. Five modii. Without it I'd be in the river.
I work where there's work: the docks, the building sites, the games.
worry: Rents. Rents rents rents. Room on the fifth floor costs what a house in the country does.

pleb: I've a room on the fourth floor of a block on the {home}. It's small, it's noisy, it's home.
My {partner} keeps me honest. The {kids} keep me poor.
Work, eat, sleep, the baths when I can. The games when they're free. It's not a bad life.
Some days are good. Today's middling.
slave: I don't have a life, stranger, I have a master. But I've friends in the household, and the Saturnalia once a year.
At the Saturnalia the masters serve us dinner. One day. It's a good day.
I was born in the house. My mother too. I've never been further than Ostia.
freed: I was a slave once. Now I'm a freedman, and my son will be a citizen born, and his son could be anything.
I still take my old master's name and go to him on holidays. That's how it's done.
I've a shop, a {partner}, and {kids}. More than I ever thought I'd have.
rich: We've the house on the {home} and a villa near Tusculum for the summer. The city in August is unbearable.
Life is duty, mostly. To the family, to the city, to the gods. And a good dinner at the end of it.
foreign: I send money home when I can. My family thinks Rome's paved with gold. It's paved with basalt.
I live near the others from my country, across the river. We have our own gods, our own food, our own gossip.
state: I serve. I get paid, I get fed, I get a pension if I live. Not many can say that.
My {partner} lives near the station. I see the {kids} when I'm off duty.
church: My life is given to God. It's simpler that way.
I was baptised at the Lateran at Easter, in the great font. Everything before that is another life.

republic: They say Caesar's taken all of Gaul and he's coming back richer than Crassus ever was.
Pompey's new theatre! Stone! With a temple on top so the old men can't pull it down.
Clodius's gangs and Milo's gangs had another fight on the Appian Way. Clodius is dead, they say. The Senate House burned with his body.
Cicero's back from exile and talking again. He never stops talking.
The price of grain's up again. The tribunes say they'll fix it. The tribunes always say that.
Crassus went east to fight the Parthians and never came back. They say they poured gold down his throat.
empire: The emperor's old and kind and never leaves Italy. Good. Emperors who travel get ideas.
Rome was nine hundred years old two years ago. The games went on for weeks.
There's new marble going up by the Colosseum. There's always new marble going up somewhere.
The Greens won six races yesterday. Six! The Blues are furious.
A block in the Subura came down in the night. Three families. The owner says it was an earthquake.
There's a Christian preacher across the river who says the world will end. Not before the games, I hope.
late: The emperor's building a new Rome in the east. We'll see how long that lasts.
The bishop's a great man now. The emperor gave him the Lateran palace and a church of gold.
They took the carvings for Constantine's arch off older monuments. Couldn't find anyone good enough to carve new ones.
The bread dole's baked bread now, not grain, and there's pork and oil on top. Can't complain.
The Senate's full of old families who still sacrifice to Jupiter and don't say so to the emperor.
fall: Narses beat the Goth king in the north. Totila's dead. Maybe now it stops.
The Pope's been in Constantinople for years. The emperor won't let him come home.
They say in the siege there were a million people here once. I've never seen more than a crowd at Mass.
The aqueducts are cut. The baths are dry. We drink from the river.
Plague, then war, then hunger, then war. God must be very angry with Rome.

republic: Jupiter on the Capitol keeps the city. Vesta keeps the fire. My household gods keep my house. Everybody has their job.
A cake for the Lares at every meal, a lamb for Jupiter on the festival. You keep the gods sweet, they keep you.
empire: Jupiter, Mars, the emperor's genius, Isis for my wife, Mithras for my brother in the army. Why choose?
The emperors become gods when they die. Well, the good ones. The bad ones just die.
late: My grandmother sacrificed to Jupiter. My mother lit candles to the martyrs. I do both, quietly.
The Christians have the emperor now. The old gods have the Senate. And the people have whatever works.
fall: God is great and Rome is small now. We pray at the tombs of the martyrs.
The old temples are shut. Some are churches now. The gods moved out and the saints moved in.

night: Get home before the thieves find you.
Mind the pots from the windows!
puzzled: Ask the Greeks, they know about that sort of thing.

moods: Can't complain, and I'm not going to.
Up since before cockcrow. My eyes are shutting as I stand.
Oh, you want to talk? Sit, sit, I've got all day. Well, not all day.
There's a lot on my mind.
A bit of wine at lunch, you know how it is.
